paragraphs.text: Heat was described long before it was measured. Physicians spoke of fevers, metalworkers judged a furnace by colour, and bakers knew an oven by how quickly flour browned in it, but none of these produced a number that one person could send to another. The first instruments that responded visibly to warmth appeared around 1600: a glass bulb with a stem standing in water, in which the liquid rose and fell as the trapped air expanded and contracted. The device was called a thermoscope, and it showed change without measuring it.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The missing piece was a scale, and a scale needs fixed points: two conditions that can be reproduced anywhere and given numbers. Candidates were plentiful and mostly poor. The temperature of a cellar, the melting of butter, the blood heat of a healthy man and the hottest summer day were all proposed, and all of them varied with the cellar, the butter, the man and the summer. What was needed was a phenomenon that happens at one temperature and no other, and there were fewer of those than the early instrument makers assumed.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Water supplied two, though not as easily as the textbooks suggest. Ice melts at a temperature that does not depend on how much ice there is, which made it an excellent lower point; water boils at a temperature that depends on the pressure of the air above it, which makes the upper point a moving target unless the pressure is specified. Early scales that ignored this disagreed by degrees between a laboratory at sea level and one in a mountain town, and the disagreement was blamed on the glassblower rather than on the mountain.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Instruments improved faster than agreement about them. The change from air to liquid removed the pressure problem inside the tube; mercury, adopted in the 1710s, expanded evenly enough over a wide range and did not wet the glass, which made a fine bore practical and a reading repeatable. By the middle of the eighteenth century a well-made instrument was more consistent than the scale it carried, and a dozen scales were in use across Europe, several of them named after the men who cut the marks.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Two of those scales survived, for reasons that had little to do with their merits. One divided the interval between the fixed points into a hundred parts and was adopted by scientific societies, then by the countries that reorganised their measures after 1790; the other used a finer division over the range of ordinary weather and was carried into use by instrument makers whose trade was with the public rather than with laboratories. Where the public and the laboratory used different scales, the public one lasted longest in the countries whose trade was strongest.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A deeper change came from thermodynamics. Work in the middle of the nineteenth century showed that temperature has a floor: there is a coldest possible state, and it sits at the same place whatever substance is used to measure. A scale that starts from that floor is not an agreement between instrument makers but a property of the world, and it made the older scales into offsets of a single one. The practical scales in use today are defined to match it as closely as measurement allows, and are revised when measurement improves.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Standardisation took another century and was driven by trade and by medicine. A steel process that must be held within five degrees, a drug that spoils above a stated temperature and a fever that means one thing at thirty-eight and another at forty all require that two instruments in different countries agree. National laboratories now maintain fixed points — the freezing of metals, the triple point of water — against which working instruments are compared, and a chain of calibrations connects a nurse’s thermometer to that definition.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The history has an unglamorous moral. The hard part was never building a device that responded to heat; a child can make a thermoscope in an afternoon. The hard part was agreeing on what the numbers meant, and that agreement took three hundred years, several false starts and a change in the underlying physics. Most of the instruments we now trust without thinking sit on top of a similar history, which is invisible precisely because it ended in agreement.
paragraphs.label: H
